title: The Second Time Zumi Closed Its Doors in Nairobi
dek: In March 2023 a Nairobi apparel marketplace that had already died once as a magazine shut for good, and its chief executive offered to vouch for its people.

story.event: Closing the B2B apparel marketplace after failing to raise funding
story.summary: Zumi, founded in Nairobi in 2016 by William McCarren and Sabrina Dorman as an online women's magazine, closed that business in 2019 for lack of advertising revenue and returned in 2020 as a B2B marketplace supplying apparel to informal retailers. In March 2023 McCarren announced on LinkedIn that Zumi was closing because it could not raise funding before reaching sustainability; about 150 jobs were reported lost, and he offered to recommend staff to other employers.
paragraphs: In March 2023 William McCarren, co-founder and chief executive of Zumi, a Nairobi company that supplied clothing stock to small shops, wrote on LinkedIn: "With a heavy heart, I share the news that ZUMI will be closing its doors." Fundraising had become extremely difficult, he wrote, and the business had not become sustainable in time to survive. Reports put the job losses at about 150.

It was the second time Zumi had closed. McCarren, who had worked at Amazon UK and Rocket Internet, quit his job in 2016 to start fashion e-commerce in Kenya. Looking for online women's magazines to partner with, he said, he found only dated print titles or content made for the West, and decided in a Nairobi Java House to build one himself. He launched Zumi with Sabrina Dorman in October 2016. It reported just under a million unique users in July 2017 and raised $250,000. Advertising never paid enough, and in November 2019 Zumi told its Instagram followers it was closing the shop.

In 2020, mid-pandemic, the name returned on a different business: a marketplace where informal clothing retailers ordered stock from suppliers through an app or a Zumi agent, with delivery by logistics partners, payment on delivery and embedded financing. Dorman stayed, joined as co-founders by Mohamed Nuur, Tomas Rosales and Eric Njogu. The last reported round, about $300,000, came in July 2021. McCarren later wrote that they had come through COVID-19, "a ban on apparel imports, and countless near-death experiences."

By early 2023 money had tightened. Citizen Digital linked a run of closures to inflation, a weakening shilling and interest rates that drew foreign investors away from frontier markets; Business Daily counted Zumi as the seventh Kenyan tech start-up to shut in about a year. McCarren said Zumi had passed $20 million in sales and 5,000 customers. By Crunchbase figures reported at the time, it had raised under $1 million since 2016.

His post thanked customers, suppliers, investors and co-founders, and then the team, whom he called hardworking and dedicated. He pointed companies that were hiring to a page of Zumi's people and asked them to message him for a recommendation. He said he would take time to reflect on what he would do differently next time.

quote.text: But a total extinction will never be its lot. Who can say that stoicism is dead? It is dead as a system; but it is alive as a virtue: its energy and vitality are still felt through many channels of life
quote.source_title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan, Project Gutenberg eBook #12096
quote.connection: Nitobe, writing as Japan's samurai order passed away, argued that a way of life can end as a system and still live on as a virtue. Zumi ended as a company. McCarren's last public act for it was to point employers towards the people who had carried its work.

reflection: Most of what Zumi built is gone: the app, the agents' rounds, the lists of suppliers. What McCarren could still do on the last day was small and specific. He thanked each group in turn, and he put his own word behind the people who had worked for him.

When something you have given yourself to ends or stalls, a project, a job, a plan, it is tempting to count the whole of it as lost. Nitobe suggests a different reckoning. The structure may go. The skill, the trust and the habits of the people involved go somewhere else, and they often travel further than the thing that once held them.
invitation: Think of one colleague who worked well beside you on something that did not last. Send them two sentences today saying specifically what they did well.

sources.title: Kenyan fashion startup ZUMI closes $250k round (6 October 2017)
sources.supports: Zumi launched in October 2016 by William McCarren and Sabrina Dorman, originally intended as fashion e-commerce; McCarren's account of quitting his job, finding only outdated print magazines or Western content, and the Java House moment in Nairobi; just under one million unique users in July 2017; the $250,000 round from Majlis Investment Management and angel investors.

sources.title: Zumi, Kenyan Based Digital Media Start-up Shuts Down (David Okelezo, 15 November 2019)
sources.supports: The first closure in November 2019, announced on Instagram ('today, we close the shop'), owing to low capital and revenue; Zumi founded by William McCarren (ex-Rocket Internet) and Sabrina Dorman; over $250,000 raised; the planned pivot to e-commerce had not happened.

sources.title: Zumi shuts down again, letting go of 150 employees (20 March 2023)
sources.supports: Closure for inability to raise funding; team of 150 laid off; McCarren's LinkedIn statement; magazine began in 2016 and shut owing to low advertising revenue; return in 2020 as a B2B marketplace (orders via app or agent, delivery through logistics partners, payment on delivery); about $970,000 disclosed funding per Crunchbase; McCarren's thanks to co-founders Mohamed Nuur, Sabrina Dorman, Tomas Rosales and Eric Njogu.

sources.title: ZUMI closes its doors as 'current macro environment makes fundraising extremely difficult' (21 March 2023)
sources.supports: Extended quotation of McCarren's LinkedIn post: 'With a heavy heart...'; over $20 million in sales and 5,000 customers; a team of 150; COVID-19, 'a ban on apparel imports, and countless near-death experiences'; thanks to customers, suppliers, investors, co-founders and the team; the people section and offer of recommendations; plans to reflect on lessons and what he would do differently.

sources.title: Seventh Kenya tech start-up goes under on lack of funding (21 March 2023)
sources.supports: At least 150 employees laid off; more than $920,000 raised since 2016 per Crunchbase; McCarren's figures of over $20 million in sales and 5,000 customers; the seventh Kenyan tech start-up to close in about a year, after Kune Foods, Notify Logistics, WeFarm, BRCK and Sky-Garden.

sources.title: E-commerce start-up Zumi closes down over lack of funding (Dennis Musau, 22 March 2023)
sources.supports: Founded in 2016; Ksh120 million ($920,000) raised per Crunchbase, the latest a Ksh39 million ($300,000) round in July 2021; shift to e-commerce because of weak advertising revenue; closures linked to inflation, a weakening currency and interest rates drawing foreign investors away from emerging and frontier economies.

sources.title: Kenyan Startup Zumi Shutting Down; 150 Employees Affected (21 March 2023)
sources.supports: Marketplace connecting apparel wholesalers with retailers with embedded financing; co-founders' roles and backgrounds (McCarren ex-Jumia; CCO Eric Njogu ex-Twiga; COO Tomas Rosales ex-BCG; CTO Mohammed Nuur ex-Amazon and SpaceX; CFO Sabrina Dorman ex-Jumia).

sources.title: Zumi: Why Nairobi-based Startup is Shutting Down (21 March 2023)
sources.supports: Employees looking for new jobs with Zumi offering recommendations; $920,000 raised over eight rounds from investors including Echo VC, Seedstars, 4Di Capital and Timon Capital.

sources.title: William McCarren (contributor profile)
sources.supports: McCarren began his career at Amazon UK and worked at Rocket Internet in Europe and East Africa; Zumi as a B2B platform for informal apparel retailers.

cross_checks.claim: Zumi was founded in 2016 by William McCarren and Sabrina Dorman as an online women's magazine
The magazine closed for lack of advertising revenue and Zumi returned in 2020 as a B2B apparel marketplace
In March 2023 McCarren announced the closure on LinkedIn, citing an inability to raise funding before reaching sustainability
Zumi had raised under $1 million in disclosed funding since 2016
McCarren offered to recommend departing staff to other employers

research_notes: Founders: the slate did not know them. Disrupt Africa (2017, quoting McCarren) and TechBuild Africa (2019) both name William McCarren and Sabrina Dorman as the founders of the 2016 magazine; McCarren's 2023 post, as reported by TechCabal, thanks four co-founders of the later marketplace (Mohamed Nuur, Sabrina Dorman, Tomas Rosales, Eric Njogu). Khusoko spells the CTO 'Mohammed Nuur'; TechCabal's spelling is used. Date: the slate gave 2022, but the closure was announced in March 2023; TechCabal reported it on the evening of 20 March, while Citizen Digital (22 March) says 'on Tuesday', so the story says only March 2023. The slate's 'funding fell through' is put as McCarren did: fundraising became extremely difficult and the business was not sustainable in time; no specific failed round is documented. Job losses: TechCabal and Business Daily report about or at least 150 laid off; McCarren's own words were that 'we built a team of 150 people', so the story says reports put the job losses at about 150. Funding: Citizen, Business Daily and Business Today give $920,000 (Ksh119-120 million) from Crunchbase, Business Today adding eight rounds; TechCabal gives about $970,000 from the same source; the story says under $1 million. The $20 million in sales and 5,000 customers are McCarren's own claims and attributed to him. The magazine's audience (just under one million unique users in July 2017) is Zumi's own figure as reported by Disrupt Africa. The first closure date comes from TechBuild Africa's report of 15 November 2019, which says the Instagram announcement was made the day before. 'A ban on apparel imports' is McCarren's phrase; he did not specify which ban, and the story does not either. McCarren said he would share reflections in the following weeks; no such post was found, so the story says only that he planned to reflect. Disrupt Africa's URL redirects to old.disruptafrica.com, which loads. The Nitobe passage concerns the passing of Bushido as an institution; it is applied by analogy.
